newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia's 1996 trade deficit seen declining.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia's 1996 trade deficit seen declining.

text.p: Malaysia's trade deficit narrowed to 523.1 million ringgit ($210 million) in November, official data released on Friday showed, setting the stage for a hefty drop in the country's 1996 trade gap.

Economists said the country was on track to record a trade deficit of under 1.5 billion ringgit ($604.5 million) last year, well below the government's forecast of 5.2 billion ringgit and the 9.3 billion ringgit recorded in 1995.
But strong economic growth and bullish forecasts for the manufacturing sector could swell the trade deficit again this year, some economists said.
November's trade gap followed a revised deficit of 782.7 million ringgit in October. Before that, Malaysia had posted surpluses in almost every month of 1996.
A Reuters poll of 10 research houses on Tuesday found they were forecasting on average a deficit of 148 million ringgit.
Although the market was expecting a smaller deficit for November, Friday's figures did not ruffle the financial markets.
The stock market was up 1.77 points at midday on Friday and the ringgit was trading at 2.4858 to the dollar, almost unchanged from the previous day.
"The November deficit was due to capital imports for the oil and gas industry in Sarawak. We are not unduly alarmed," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at stockbrokers HG Asia in Singapore.
"The December figures should show the deficit for the whole of 1996 to be around 1.2-1.3 billion ringgit. This will be better than the full year projection by the Ministry of Finance," he added.

In the Reuters poll, economists on average expected a deficit of 1.28 billion ringgit for 1996, although their estimates varied between a shortfall of 2.5 billion ringgit and a surplus of 500 million.
With the value of imports reduced by the strengthening ringgit, some economists said a pick-up in exports would be the main factor in reducing the trade deficit this year.
"The deficit will start to improve once exports improve," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But other economists said a rise in manufactured exports would likely be accompanied by an even faster rise in imported intermediate and capital goods.
J.M. Sassoon & Co's chief economist, Liew Yin Sze, said: "In 1997, I'm looking at some increase in the current account (deficit) in the second half, mainly because of the strong domestic economy.
"The manufacturing sector is still very strong compared with elsewhere in the region."

Strong export growth will traditionally be accompanied by even stronger import growth, Liew said, as imported components form a large chunk of exports, particularly in the electronics and electrical sector.

Malaysia's International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz said on Thursday the manufacturing sector would grow by 12.5 percent this year, marginally slower than 1996's 12.8 percent and against 14.5 percent in 1995.
